In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In this there are four issues.

The first: al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring. So Allah the Exalted revealed: "Woe to those who give less," and after that they gave the best measure. Al-Farra' said: they became among the most complete in measure up to this day. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It was the first surah revealed upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he came to Medina, and this practice was among them: when they bought, they took in full with a heavy measure, but when they sold, they reduced the measure and the scale. Some said: it was revealed concerning a man known as Abu Juhaynah, whose name was 'Amr, who had two sa' measures: he took with one and gave with the other. That is, it nearly fills but does not do so, and the meaning is that you are close to one another, so no one has merit over another except through piety. The fourth: The mutaffif is the one who gives less in measuring and weighing, and does not give in full as we have explained. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik that he recited "Woe to those who give less" and said: Do not cheat, and do not adulterate [[Thus in the originals: i.e., do not deceive. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But when they measure or weigh for them, they give less﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His words, "When they measure or weigh for them": i.e., they measured for them or weighed for them, so the lam was omitted, and the verb became transitive and governed the accusative. Similar is nasahtuka and nasahtu laka, and amartuka bihi and amartukahu. This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Farra'. He said: I bear witness that he is in the Fire. al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin woman say: Do not seek manliness from one whose manliness is at the tops of measures and the tongues of scales. This is from the speech of the people of the Hijaz and those neighbouring them from Qays. al-Zajjaj said: it is not permissible to pause on "kalu" and "wazanu" until you join "hum" to it. He said: Some people make it an emphasis and permit pausing on "kalu" and "wazanu." The first is the preferred view, because it is one word. This is the view of al-Kisa'i. Abu 'Ubayd said: 'Isa ibn 'Umar used to make them two words, pausing on "kalu" and "wazanu" and beginning with "hum yukhsirun." He said: I think Hamzah's recitation is also like that. Abu 'Ubayd said: The preferred view is that they are one word, for two reasons. The first: the script, since they wrote them without an alif; had they been separate, they would be written "kalu" and "wazanu" with an alif. The second: it is said "kiltuka" and "wazantuka," meaning "kiltu laka" and "wazantu laka," and this is good Arabic, as one says "sidtuka" and "sidtu laka," "kasabtuka" and "kasabtu laka," and likewise "shakartuka" and "nasahtuka," and similar. His words: "yukhsirun" means they diminish, and the Arabs say: akhsartu al-mizan and khasirtuhu. "Hum" is in the accusative position, according to the reading of the majority, referring to the people: the sense is "when they measure [for] the people or weigh for them, they give less." In this there are two views. One is that it means "they measured for them or weighed for them," so the preposition is omitted and the verb reaches its object, as the poet said:

"Indeed I gathered for you aknu' and 'asaqil,
and indeed I forbade you from the daughters of al-awbar."

He meant: "I gathered for you." The other view is that it is by omitting the modified noun and placing the modified-to in its place, and the modified noun is "the measured" and "the weighed." From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): "You, the assembly of non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters by which those before you were destroyed: the measure and the scale." He singled out the non-Arabs because they used to combine measuring and weighing together, whereas these were separate in the two sanctuaries: the people of Mecca weighed, and the people of Medina measured.

On the second reading, "hum" is in the nominative position as the subject, meaning: "when they measure for people or weigh for them, then they give less." This is not sound, because the first would then be left without a predicate; it would only be correct if after it were: "when they measure, they themselves give less," or "when they weigh, they themselves give less."

The second issue: Ibn 'Abbas said the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Five for five: no people break a covenant except that Allah sets their enemy over them; nor do they judge by other than what Allah has revealed except that poverty spreads among them; nor does immorality appear among them except that plague appears among them; nor do they cheat in measure except that they are denied vegetation and seized by years of drought; nor do they withhold zakat except that Allah withholds rain from them." Abu Bakr al-Bazzar recorded it in this meaning, and Malik ibn Anas also from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar. We have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah. Malik ibn Dinar said: I entered upon a neighbour of mine whom death had come to, and he kept saying: "Two mountains of fire! Two mountains of fire!" I said: What are you saying? Are you delirious? [[hajara in his sleep and illness, yahjuru hajran: he raved.]] He said: O Abu Yahya, I had two measures: I measured with one and took with the other. I got up and began striking one against the other until I broke them. He said: O Abu Yahya, every time I struck one against the other, it grew larger, and he died of his pain. Ikrimah said: I bear witness against every measurer or weigher that he is in the Fire. It was said to him: But your son is a measurer or weigher. He said: I bear witness that he is in the Fire. al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin woman say: Do not seek manliness from one whose manliness is at the tops of measures and the tongues of scales. This is also narrated from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). 'Abd Khayr said: 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a man who was weighing saffron and had tipped the scale; so he overturned the scale and said: "Establish the weighing with justice, then tip it afterwards as you wish." It is as if he ordered him to level it first so that he would become accustomed to it, and the obligatory would be distinguished from the voluntary. Nafi' said: Ibn 'Umar would pass by a seller and say: "Fear Allah and give full measure and weight with justice, for the cheats on the Day of Resurrection will be held back until sweat bridles them up to the middle of their ears." It has also been narrated that Abu Hurayrah came to Medina when the Prophet (ﷺ) had gone out to Khaybar and had appointed Siba' ibn 'Urfutah over Medina. Abu Hurayrah said: "We found him in the dawn prayer; he recited in the first rak'ah Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, and in the second rak'ah 'Woe to those who give less.'" Abu Hurayrah said: "So I say in my prayer: 'Woe to the father of so-and-so, who had two measures: when he took by measure, he took in full, and when he gave by measure, he gave less.'"

Denunciation and great astonishment at their condition, in their audacity regarding fraud (taṭfīf), as if they do not bring the fraud to mind, nor do they conjecture (at all) (that they will be raised up) and so be questioned about what they do. Here "ẓann" (conjecture) carries the sense of certainty (yaqīn), meaning: will those people not be certain? And if they were certain, they would not have diminished in measure and weight. It has also been said: "ẓann" here means doubt (taraddud), meaning: if they are not certain of the resurrection, then let them at least conjecture it, so that they reflect, investigate it, and take the more cautious course (for a great day), whose matter is great, namely the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾. In it there are four issues.

The first: the governing element (ʿāmil) of "yawm" (day) is a hidden verb, indicated by "mab'ūthūn" (raised). The meaning is: they will be raised on the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for "yawm" in "li-yawmin ʿaẓīm" (for a great day), and it is indeclinable (mabnī). It has been said that it is in the genitive position, because it has been added to a non-declinable word. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning "on a day"; it is said: "Stay until the day when so-and-so goes out," so you put "yawm" in the accusative; but if they add it to a noun, then they put it in the genitive and say: "Stay until the day of so-and-so's going out." It has also been said that there is inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr) in the statement, its estimate being: "Indeed they will be raised on the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds, for a great day."

The second: It is related from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān that a Bedouin said to him: "I have heard what Allah, exalted is He, said about the defrauders (al-muṭaffifīn)." He meant by that that this great threat which you have heard of has been directed at the defrauders; "so what is your opinion of yourself, while you take the wealth of the Muslims without measure or weight?" In this denunciation and astonishment, and in the word "ẓann," and in the description of the day as "great," and of mankind standing in it humbly before Allah, and in the description of Him as "Lord of the worlds," there is an eloquent exposition of the greatness of the sin and the gravity of the wrong in fraud, and of what is in the like of his situation of injustice, and of the abandonment of upholding justice (qist), and of acting upon equity and fairness in every giving and taking, indeed in every word and deed.

The third: Ibn ʿUmar recited: "Woe to the defrauders," until he reached "the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds," and he wept until he fell down, and he refrained from reciting what followed. Then he said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds, a day whose measure is fifty thousand years; some of them the sweat reaches to their ankles, some to their knees, some to their waist, some to their chest, some to their ears, until one of them is submerged in his sweat as the frog is submerged [[i.e., in water.]]." And some people related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "They stand for a measure of three hundred years." He said: "And it is made light for the believers, to the extent of their obligatory prayer." It is related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "They stand for a thousand years in the shade." Mālik related from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "On the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds, until one of them stands in his sweat up to the middle of his ears." And from him also, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "He stands a hundred years." Abū Hurayrah said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Bashīr al-Ghifārī: "How will you act on a day when mankind stands in it for a measure of three hundred years before the Lord of the worlds, no news reaches them in it, and no command is given in it?" Bashīr said: "Allah is the one sought for help." I say: We have mentioned it as a raised (marfūʿ) report from the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed it is lightened for the believer, until it is lighter for him than the obligatory prayer he performed in the world." [Concerning] "a questioner asked" [[See vol. 18, p. 282.]] [al-Maʿārij: 1]. And from Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is made easy for the believers, to the extent of their obligatory prayer." It has been said: that station for the believer is like the decline of the sun. The evidence for this from the Book is His statement, the Truth: "Indeed the friends of Allah—no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve" [Yūnus: 62], then He described them, saying: "Those who believed and used to fear Allah" [Yūnus: 63]. May Allah make us among them by His grace, generosity, bounty and kindness. Āmīn.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "mankind" (al-nās) is Jibrīl (peace be upon him), who stands before the Lord of the worlds; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. But it is far-fetched, because of the reports we have mentioned on this, and they are sound and established; and it is sufficient for you what is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning "the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds": he said: "One of them stands in his sweat up to the middle of his ears." Then it has been said: this standing is on the day when they rise from their graves. It has also been said: it is in the Hereafter, concerning the rights of His servants in the world. Yazīd al-Rashk said: they stand before Him for judgment.

The fourth: Standing for Allah, Lord of the worlds, glory be to Him, is insignificant in comparison with His greatness and His right. As for people standing for one another, scholars differed concerning it: some permitted it, and some forbade it. It has been related that the Prophet (ﷺ) rose for Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib and embraced him, and Ṭalḥah rose for Kaʿb ibn Mālik on the day he was forgiven (repentance accepted). And the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the Anṣār when Saʿd ibn Muʿādh came upon him: "Stand up for your master (qūmū ilā sayyidikum)." He also said: "Whoever is pleased that people should stand for him, let him take his seat in the Fire." This returns to the state of the man and his intention: if he expects it and regards it as his due, it is forbidden; but if it is in the manner of cheerfulness and kinship, it is permissible, especially upon occasions such as returning from travel and the like. Some of this has passed at the end of Sūrat Yūsuf [[See vol. 9, p. 265 onward.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾. Some scholars of the Arabic language said: *kalla* (nay) is a word of deterrence and admonition, meaning: the matter is not as they are upon, of cheating in measure and weight, or denying the Hereafter, so let them desist from that. It is a word of deterrence and rebuke. Then he resumed and said: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked﴾. Al-Hasan said: *kalla* means *haqqan* (truly). Some people narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning *kalla* that he said: "Do you not believe?" Accordingly, the pause (*waqf*) is at ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾. In the tafsir of Muqatil: "Indeed, the deeds of the wicked." Some people narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Indeed, the souls of the wicked and their deeds are in Sijjin." Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that he said: "Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth, which is turned over, and the record of the wicked is placed beneath it." Similar was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Ka'b. Ka'b said: "Beneath it are the souls of the disbelievers, beneath the cheek of Iblis." Also from Ka'b: "Sijjin is a black rock beneath the seventh earth, on which is written the name of every devil, and the souls of the disbelievers are cast beside it." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Sijjin is beneath the cheek of Iblis." Yahya ibn Sallam said: "It is a black stone beneath the earth, on which the souls of the disbelievers are recorded." 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: "It is the lowest seventh earth, and in it are Iblis and his offspring." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Indeed, when the disbeliever is about to die, the messengers of Allah attend him, but they cannot, because of Allah's hatred of him and their hatred of him, either delay or hasten it until its appointed hour comes. When its hour comes, they seize his soul and raise it to the angels of punishment, who show him what Allah wills of evil. Then they descend with it to the seventh earth, which is Sijjin, and it is the last domain of Iblis, and there they register his record." Concerning this verse, Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Indeed, when the soul of the wicked person is taken, it is carried up to the heaven, but the heaven refuses to accept it. Then it is brought down to the earth, but the earth refuses to accept it. So it enters the seven earths, until it reaches Sijjin, which is the cheek of Iblis. "How often has a sin covered over the heart of a wicked man, / Then he repented of the sin that had covered him and was lifted away."

"Rānat al-khamru ʿalā ʿaqlihi": i.e., wine overcame his intellect. "Rāna ʿalayhi al-nuʿās": when it covered him. From this is ʿUmar's saying about al-Usayfiʿ (Usayfiʿ of Juhaynah): "fa-aṣbaḥa qad rīna bihi" (so he became overcome by it), i.e., debts overcame him, and he was in debt. From this is also Abu Zubayd's description of a man who drank until wine overcame him in drunkenness, when he said:

"Then, when he saw him, wine overcame him / and it was not to be warded off by caution."

So his saying "rānat bihi al-khamr" means: wine overcame his intellect and heart. Al-Umawi said: "Qad arāna al-qawm, fa-hum murīnūn," when their livestock perished and became emaciated. This is one of the matters that comes upon them and overpowers them, so they cannot bear it. Abu Zayd said: it is said, "qad rīna bi-l-rajul raynan," when he falls into something from which he cannot escape and has no means against it. Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi said: al-Rayn is that the heart blackens from sins; al-Tabʿ (sealing) is that it is sealed upon the heart, and this is more severe than rayn; and al-Iqfāl (locking) is more severe than sealing. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Rayn is like rust that covers the heart like a thin cloud; similar is al-Ghayn: it is said, "ghīna ʿalā qalbihi," meaning it was covered. Al-Ghayn is also a dense tree, singular ghaynāʾ, i.e., green, abundant in leaves, with intertwined branches.

The saying of al-Farra' has already been mentioned: that it is the surrounding of the heart by sin. Al-Tha'labi related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim," i.e., it covered over them. This is the sound report from him, if Allah wills.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Aʿmash, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal read "rāna" with imalah (inclination), because the first radical of the verb is rāʾ and its middle radical, the alif, is converted from a yāʾ, so imalah is good for that. Whoever reads it with fatḥah (open vowel) follows the original form, because the pattern of the first radical in fa'ala is fatḥah, like kāla and bāʿa and the like. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred this.

Ḥafṣ paused on "bal," then began "rāna" with a pause that makes the lām clear, not for silence.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: when He veiled them in this world from the light of His oneness, He veiled them in the Hereafter from seeing Him.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary on al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, Surah 83, verses 18–21:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾. *Kallā* (كَلَّا) means "truly," and the pause is at *tukadhdhibūn* (تُكَذِّبُونَ). It has also been said that it means: the matter is not as they say, nor as they assume; rather, their record is in *Sijjīn* (سِجِّينٌ), and the record of the believers is in *ʿIlliyyūn*. Muqatil said: *kallā* means they do not believe in the punishment they will endure. Then He began a new statement: "Indeed, the record of the righteous is elevated in *ʿIlliyyūn* according to their rank." Ibn ʿAbbas said: that is, in Paradise. And from him also: their deeds are in the Book of God in the heaven. Al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatada said: it means the seventh heaven, in which are the spirits of the believers. Ibn al-Ajlah narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: it is the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (*Sidrat al-Muntahā*), at which every matter from God's command ends and does not pass beyond. They say: "My Lord! Your servant so-and-so," and He knows him better than they do. Then a book from God, the Mighty and Majestic, sealed with His security from punishment, comes to him. This is His saying: ﴿Nay! Indeed, the record of the righteous﴾.

From Kaʿb al-Ahbar, who said: when the soul of the believer is taken, it is raised up to the heaven, the gates of the heaven are opened for it, and the angels receive it with glad tidings. Then they go with it until they reach the Throne. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 83, verses 29–36:

God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who committed sin﴾ describe the disbelievers in this world, along with the believers, through their mockery of them. The intended meaning is the leaders of Quraysh from among the people of polytheism.
